name: Fur and leather working for clothing at Contrebandiers Cave
summary: Bone tools and skinned carnivore bones from Contrebandiers Cave, Morocco, suggest people were preparing furs and leather, probably for clothing, 120,000 to 90,000 years ago.
description: Deposits at Contrebandiers Cave on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, dated between 120,000 and 90,000 years ago, hold bone tools likely used for working leather and fur, together with carnivore bones bearing skinning marks. The excavators call this highly suggestive proxy evidence for clothing; no clothing itself survives.

impact.note: Covering the body with prepared skins is a new capability, but the evidence is for one region and the sources do not show that later clothing elsewhere descended from this community, so reach and generativity are scored low.

date.label: 120,000 to 90,000 years ago
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Bone tools from Contrebandiers Cave on the Atlantic coast of Morocco are dated between 120,000 and 90,000 years ago, which is about 118,050 to 88,050 BCE when converted by subtracting from 1950.

evidence.supports: Here we describe a bone tool tradition from Contrebandiers Cave on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, dated between 120,000-90,000 years ago

date.label: 120,000 to 90,000 years ago
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: The excavators read the carnivore bones with skinning marks and the bone tools likely used for fur processing, from the same deposits, as highly suggestive proxy evidence of clothing; the date range is that of the deposits, 120,000 to 90,000 years ago (about 118,050 to 88,050 BCE).

evidence.supports: The combination of carnivore bones with skinning marks and bone tools likely used for fur processing provide highly suggestive proxy evidence for the earliest clothing in the archaeological record.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The clothing is inferred from tools and skinning marks; the authors themselves call it proxy evidence.
The Schöningen evidence (Leiden University, 2022) needs its own card, and whether it shows clothing or sleeping skins is not settled by the sources read.
The date of the clothing louse split (the paper cites Toups et al. 2011 for an origin as early as 170,000 years ago) is not evidence for this site and was not used.

Whether later clothing traditions descend from this one is unknown, which is why reach and generativity are low; the lead curator may prefer a broader record for clothing among early Homo sapiens if a source for the louse evidence is added.

research.note: The 2021 paper calls this proxy evidence for the earliest clothing in the archaeological record, but Leiden University reports cut-marked bear bones at Schöningen in Germany, about 300,000 years old, as evidence of prehistoric clothing, so whether this community was first or learned it from others is not settled.
